title: STAR-FL: Secure Federated Learning with Spatial-Temporal Analysis and Robust Aggregation

C-a.quote: Updates that are identified as malicious by both spatial and temporal analyses are removed from that round. Third, we aggregate the remaining model updates while adjusting the server learning rate based on the sum of update signs.
C-a.locator: Section V Overview of STAR-FL and Algorithm 1; three defense-purposed mechanisms act on the same round, and each has its purpose stated in its own subsection. Spatial: "We apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the last layer updates ∇Wti to utilize this difference for detecting poisoned updates.". Temporal: "To identify attackers based on the patterns of their historical updates, we perform per-client temporal analysis.", with its own decision rule, "A lower similarity implies that the client’s current behavior is inconsistent with its past behavior, which flags it as a potentially malicious client.". Robust aggregation: "C. Robust Aggregation In this step, we employ an additional defense mechanism by utilizing adaptive server learning rates. Unlike traditional approaches that maintain a fixed learning rate during aggregation, we dynamically adjust the learning rates across different training rounds. This approach further enhances the robustness of the global model by mitigating the influence of malicious updates.". The two filters are DISTINCT under the granularity rule and not two stages of one signal: they compute different statistics (PCA plus K-means on last-layer updates across CLIENTS; an exponential moving average plus KDE on cosine similarity across ROUNDS), each flags its own malicious cluster, and the quoted sentence composes their two decisions conjunctively. Amendment 3 needs no excision -- all three purposes are stated in defense terms in the Abstract, "First, we employ spatial-temporal clustering to identify and remove potentially malicious updates from the FL training process. Second, we adjust the learning rate during aggregation to mitigate the impact of any malicious updates that evade detection."

C-b.quote: First, we employ spatial-temporal clustering to identify and remove potentially malicious updates from the FL training process. Second, we adjust the learning rate during aggregation to mitigate the impact of any malicious updates that evade detection.
C-b.locator: Abstract; the pairing reason is RESIDUAL COVERAGE stated for the paper's own constituents -- the detector removes what it can identify and the aggregation stage exists to absorb what evades it -- and it is restated in the Conclusion, "Third, we integrate a robust aggregation strategy that adaptively adjusts the learning rates for client updates to mitigate the influence of adversarial contributions that evade detection.", and read back off the results, "Overall, these findings highlight that STAR-FL benefits from the complementary strengths of spatial-temporal filtering and robust aggregation, while offering flexible defense depending on dataset complexity.". PROVENANCE CHECK PASSES: the deficiency-of-alternatives sentence in Section II is about PRIOR work, "are typically effective only when the number of malicious clients is very small, and residual poisoned updates may still degrade global model performance.", but the pairing reason above is stated for STAR-FL's own two stages in three separate places, so C-b does not rest on the critique of others

C-c.quote: c) Attack Success Rate: the percentage of base class samples that are classified into the attacker-specified target class in the presence of a trigger.
C-c.locator: Section VI-A Metrics; the assembled framework's own MA/BA/ASR are reported against six baseline defenses -- "TABLE II: Effectiveness of our proposed defense compared to existing defenses. ↑ denotes better performance with higher values, and ↓ denotes better performance with lower values." -- across FMNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, at three malicious-client fractions, under four attacks ("TABLE VI: Main task accuracy, base class accuracy, and attack success rate under different attacks.") and under two Dirichlet heterogeneity levels ("The results in Table V show that greater heterogeneity degrades accuracy and increases ASR.")

C-d.quote: Effectiveness of Robust Aggregation. We further examined the performance of STAR-FL by incorporating robust aggregation with spatial and temporal filtering. Table IV highlights the results for these defense settings. ... Robust aggregation alone reduced the ASR most effectively to 1.30%, though at the cost of a lower base class accuracy. ... Robust aggregation alone provided the best balance, achieving the highest main task accuracy (75.32%) and keeping the ASR low (4.70%), while also maintaining a competitive base class accuracy (57.40%).
C-d.locator: Section VI-D Ablation Studies, "TABLE IV: Main task accuracy, base class accuracy, and attack success rate under different combinations of spatialtemporal filtering and robust aggregation.". THIS IS A TEXTBOOK C-d AND IT IS THE MIRROR IMAGE OF DROP's DROPlet ARM. Table IV has three arms -- spatial+robust, temporal+robust, and robust aggregation alone -- in which the DOWNSTREAM mechanism (the sign-based adaptive server learning rate) is present and unmodified in every arm, the attack and the malicious fraction are fixed, and the ONLY thing that varies is which upstream filter feeds it: spatial, temporal, or none. That is three upstream conditions with the downstream held fixed, and the composed system's own MA/BA/ASR read at each. A second independent route is Table III, "TABLE III: Main task accuracy, base class accuracy, and attack success rate under different combinations of spatial and temporal filtering.", which varies the upstream filter (spatial, temporal, both) with no robust aggregation, i.e. a fixed FedAvg-style downstream. Both tables are labelled ablations and both happen to remove an UPSTREAM stage, which is why they satisfy C-d where DROP's leave-one-out (which removes the DOWNSTREAM distillation stage) does not

C-e.quote: Overall, these findings highlight that STAR-FL benefits from the complementary strengths of spatial-temporal filtering and robust aggregation, while offering flexible defense depending on dataset complexity. ... On simpler datasets such as FMNIST, spatial-temporal filtering provides limited benefit and robust aggregation alone outperforms STAR-FL in terms of ASR. In contrast, the full framework provides greater benefits on complex datasets such as CIFAR-10.
C-e.locator: Section VI-D; the claim says what each constituent contributes to the composed outcome and makes the contribution CONDITIONAL ON THE DATASET, and the mechanism is named elsewhere in the same subsection -- "This trade-off highlights the difficulty of distinguishing malicious updates from benign updates in high-dimensional settings, where stricter filtering improves robustness but reduces accuracy." and "These findings indicate that the integration of robust aggregation suppresses ASR, though sometimes at the cost of accuracy.". Further constituent-level attributions: "These results indicate that both defenses are highly effective on simpler datasets, with temporal filtering providing a small advantage in terms of robustness." and "By integrating spatial–temporal filtering with robust aggregation, STAR-FL establishes a more reliable and stronger defense framework for federated learning."

coder_note:
THE FRAME'S FIRST EXTERNALLY MEASURED REVERSAL IN THE ORDERING OF COMPOSED ARMS, AND THE PAPER STATES IT AS ITS OWN CONCLUSION. Table IV holds the downstream mechanism fixed and varies the upstream filter across three conditions, and the resulting ranking of composed pipelines is not the same on the two datasets. The paper says so in one sentence: "On simpler datasets such as FMNIST, spatial-temporal filtering provides limited benefit and robust aggregation alone outperforms STAR-FL in terms of ASR. In contrast, the full framework provides greater benefits on complex datasets such as CIFAR-10.". On FMNIST the arm with NO upstream filter is the best of the composed arms on ASR -- "Robust aggregation alone reduced the ASR most effectively to 1.30%, though at the cost of a lower base class accuracy." -- against 3.60% for the full framework in Table II; on CIFAR-10 the ordering goes the other way, with robust aggregation alone at 4.70% -- "Robust aggregation alone provided the best balance, achieving the highest main task accuracy (75.32%) and keeping the ASR low (4.70%), while also maintaining a competitive base class accuracy (57.40%)." -- against 4.10% for the full framework. So an independent group, on its own pipeline, measured a composed-arm ordering that changes with the dataset, and read it as a scope condition on its own design rather than as a defect. THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE THE AUDIT HAS FOUND FOR ANSWERING THE NOVELTY AND EXTERNAL-VALIDITY CHARGE AT ONCE, and A3 should cite it directly: our claim is not that composition-dependence is exotic, it is that nobody measures it as the object.

WHAT IT DOES NOT LICENCE, STATED SO THE ROUND CANNOT OVERSELL IT. These are single-run point estimates -- no seeds, no intervals, and no statement of variance anywhere in the paper (the setup is "We consider 20 clients in our setting, with 50% of the clients randomly chosen in each round to participate in the FL process. The attackers insert a plus pattern as a trigger (Fig. 1) into all samples of a specific class (base class) to poison the local datasets following the BadNets [24] attack."), and the gaps in question are 1.5 points of ASR on FMNIST and 0.6 on CIFAR-10. Under the standard app:sixcell already applies to the EMNIST cell, that is NOT a demonstrated reversal: two intervals must exclude zero and the signs must differ. So this row is external corroboration that the phenomenon is visible in other people's data and is NOT a second sign reversal, must not be counted as one, and must not be described as replication. The right sentence for A3 is that a defense paper's own ablation already shows its composed ranking depending on the dataset, reported without intervals and without follow-up.

C-d = YES, AND THE PAIR WITH DROP IS THE BEST TEACHING EXAMPLE IN THE FRAME FOR WHY THE RUBRIC'S DIRECTION CLAUSE IS NOT A TECHNICALITY. Both papers run a leave-one-out ablation over a two-stage detect-then-aggregate pipeline; both call it an ablation; both report composed MA/ASR for every arm. DROP removes the DOWNSTREAM stage (distillation) and cannot identify how the downstream stage responds to its input, so C-d = NO and it carries a primary. STAR-FL removes the UPSTREAM stage and can, so C-d = YES and it does not. The two arms are complements of each other in the same 2x2, which is exactly why the rubric had to fix the direction in advance -- with the word ablation alone, these two rows would have received the same code. A5 should print them side by side.

STAR-FL ALSO SUPPLIES THE FRAME'S CLEANEST INSTANCE OF THE COST OF NOT HAVING THE OTHER HALF. The paper has three upstream conditions crossed with two downstream conditions (Table III = filters with plain aggregation, Table IV = filters with robust aggregation), which is a genuine 3x2 design in substance -- but the two tables are never crossed in one place, the no-filter/no-robust cell is Table II's FedAvg row, and the full spatial+temporal+robust cell lives in a third table. The interaction is therefore present in the data and never computed. This is a variant of PRoVeFL's missing cell: there the cell was absent, here the cells exist in three different tables and are never differenced. A4 can use both, and should use PRoVeFL first because its missing cell is one bar.

DOMAIN AND SCOPE NOTES. Metrics include BASE CLASS ACCURACY alongside MA and ASR, which is a third axis most of the frame does not report, and the trade-off the paper repeatedly finds is between ASR and BA rather than ASR and MA -- "This trade-off highlights the difficulty of distinguishing malicious updates from benign updates in high-dimensional settings, where stricter filtering improves robustness but reduces accuracy.". Worth one line in A5, because the composed arms it ranks differently would rank differently again on BA. The CIFAR-100 arm uses a different architecture from the other two datasets, "Finally, we use a ResNet-18 architecture to train the CIFAR-100 dataset.", so the paper's dataset comparison is not architecture-controlled; our own cell 7 holds the architecture fixed while changing the dataset, which is a difference in our favour and should be stated in the same breath as the citation.
